newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese liquor makers face competiton from beer.
newsitem.headline: Chinese liquor makers face competiton from beer.

text.p: Chinese distilleries are facing greater competition from breweries as more people abandon the traditional drink of spirits in favour of beer, analysts and company officials said on Monday.
Demand for beer has been increasing steadily, preventing distilleries from expanding their operations, they told the Hong Kong-based newsletter China Securities Bulletin.
"Breweries have brighter futures than distilleries," said Jin Xianming, a Shenzhen J&A Securities analyst who specialises in China's beverage industry.

Domestic liquor production has slowed in the past few years as the result of changing tastes and Beijing's policy to limit distilleries, which consume large amounts of grain considered vital to feed China's 1.2 billion people, analysts said.

A recent report released by a top think-tank, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, forecast China's grain shortfall would hit 50 million tonnes by the year 2030 with estimated annual consumption of 700 million tonnes.
China's liquor output rose about three percent year-on-year in 1996, compard with an average growth rate of 10 percent between 1987 and 1994, official figures showed.
"Supply has exceeded demand (in the domestic liquor market)," said an official at Shenzhen-listed Anhui Gujing Distillery Co Ltd.
Some 40,000 distilleries in China produced six million tonnes of liquor last year, according to official statistics.
"Little growth is seen in the earnings of distilleries over the next few years," the Gujing official said. "Listed distillery firms need to diversify to survive competition."
There are a handful of distilleries listed on China's two stock exchanges in Shenzhen and Shanghai, including Luzhou Old-cellar Co Ltd, Hunan Jiuguijiu Co Ltd and Sichuan Tuopai Yeast Liquor Co Ltd.
"We plan to buy a local brewery with proceeds from a forthcoming offer of new B shares for further diversification," the Gujing official said without elaborating.
Gujing late last year paid 38 million yuan ($4.6 million) for an 80 percent stake in a local wine producer, using proceeds from its initial public offering of 18 million domestic currency A shares.
China's major distilleries have also seen their profits drained by producers of fake name-brand liquor, which have mushroomed in recent years, analysts said.
"This (fake liquor) is a serious problem ... it has cost listed distillery companies a lot of money, " said analyst Jin.
"We have set up a department exclusively for wiping out liquors that illegally use our brands," the Gujing official said.
Analysts and officials generally played down competition from imported liquors, which have declined in popularity due to of hefty prices in China.
"Most Chinese still can not afford to drink foreign liquors," an analyst at China Guotai Securities said.
"Some Chinese think foreign liquors look better but taste worse," he added.
Chinese distilleries are moving to produce lower-proof as well as higher quality liquors to cater to changing tastes, analysts said.
"The cheap liquor market has reached its saturation point and competition in that sector is high," Jiuguijiu said in a recently released share prospectus.
Higher-priced, quality liquors accounted for about 10 percent of national annual output in recent years, official figures showed.
Liquor has traditionally been most popular in northern China, where colder weather has supported demand, analysts said.
But lower-proof spirits, which are usually more expensive, have recently seen stronger demand in southern and eastern China due to rising incomes, they said.
(US$1=8.3 yuan)
